notes: "A strange action that takes place is something that shouldn't have happened (but it did). This is a strange incident. The difference between this and 事変 is that while 事変 can also be used to describe a strange incident, it also can be used to talk about another type of incident as well. For example, the ""Manshuu Jihen"" is the ""Manshuu Incident."" This word, 変事 is more just a strange or unusual incident." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

notes:
"The chief father isn't your own father, but he is the chief of your father. He's your father's older brother, who has always owned your father. He's your uncle. This word can be used for your mother's brother too, but in both cases he has to be the older brother, not younger." "The reading for this is an exception, at least the 父 part is, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember:Your uncle is a very religious man, he is the chief, after all. Whenever you see him he's always shouting, ""Oh Jesus! (おじ)"" at the sky. Your uncle and Jesus are pretty close."

"An uncle on your father's side is still your uncle. This uncle always has to be younger than him though. " "The reading for this word is an exception. But you already learned the 伯父 which means uncle too. Well they have the same reading! So if you know one uncle, you know them all!"

notes: "This word follows the ""number of things"" pattern where there's a kanji for a number plus つ on the end. Whenever you see this, you know the word means ""____ things."" Knowing that, as long as you know the kanji (which you do) you can figure out what number of things it is. For this one, it's the kanji for eight plus つ. So, this one is eight things." "Since all of the ""number of things"" words all follow the same pattern (number plus つ), you really just have to remember the part before the つ (and then remember that the つ is in all of these). All of the readings are the kun'yomi reading, which means we'll have to use a mnemonic to remember them (you know the on'yomi reading of the kanji portion).So what eight things do you have? You have eight yachts (やっつ). Go ahead and count them. They're beautiful. Also, be sure not to be confused by this particular reading mnemonic. It includes the つ, even though the つ is outside the reading you need to learn (just makes things easier for you overall). Since you can see the つ outside, it shouldn't be too difficult for you."

So in this case, you know that this word means woman." "When a word is a single kanji with no okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it tends to use a kun'yomi reading. It's just you and her in the store, and you're staring each other down. Oh. It turns out she's the store owner (おんな), which is weird, because you are in a store that makes only manly things. A woman owner of a manly things store? Strange..."

example_sentences.japanese: あの女はだれ？
example_sentences.english: Who is that woman?

example_sentences.japanese: わたしは女です。
example_sentences.english: I'm a woman.

example_sentences.japanese: おれはこどもをせわする女がほしい。
example_sentences.english: I want a woman who will help look after my children.

notes: "月 in Japanese means ""moon"" but it also means ""month."" Why? Probably because the moon takes about a month to get through its cycles. So, what's the fourth moon of the year? Here's a hint, it's the same as the fourth month of the year: April." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.Also, this is a specific month, so it uses the がつ reading."

example_sentences.japanese: たんじょうびは、四月九日です。
example_sentences.english: My birthday is April ninth.

example_sentences.japanese: 四月はさくらがさくので、王子は日本にいきたがっています。
example_sentences.english: Since cherry blossoms are in bloom in April, the prince wants to go to Japan.

example_sentences.japanese: 四月にりょうしんがりこんしたストレスで、おれのガールフレンドにはすこしひげがはえた。
example_sentences.english: My girlfriend suffered from so much stress after her parents divorced in April that she started to grow a little bit of a mustache.

notes: "This vocab word and the kanji that makes it have the same meaning: Circle." The reading you learned for this kanji is the kun'yomi one. Since this vocab word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Guess what? That means you already know it!

example_sentences.japanese: これは、ピカソがえがいた丸です。
example_sentences.english: This is a circle painted by Picasso.

example_sentences.japanese: このちずにかいてある丸はなんですか。
example_sentences.english: What's this circle drawn on the map?

example_sentences.japanese: わたしのくろラブは、おどろいて、めが丸になった。
example_sentences.english: My black lab was shocked and his eyes bulged wide open.

notes: "This vocab made up of a single kanji shares its meaning with said single kanji. That meaning is dog." Since this is a word made up of a single kanji and nothing else, you can assume that this word will use the kun'yomi reading. The reading you learned for this kanji happens to be the kun'yomi reading as well. So if you know the kanji you know the reading.

example_sentences.japanese: 犬とねこがいます。
example_sentences.english: There is a dog and a cat.

example_sentences.japanese: その王は犬を六ぴきかっています。
example_sentences.english: That king has six dogs.

example_sentences.japanese: わたしの犬は、白さいがすきだ。
example_sentences.english: My dog likes Chinese cabbage.

english: Eight Days, Day Eight, Eighth Day
notes: "Eighth day or day eight. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense." "Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:Every eight days you have to buy yogurt to fuel your car (ようか). Your car runs on yogurt, but it needs to be refilled every eight days to keep running. It's really inconvenient because it's just ONE day more than a week. And a week just feels better. Oh well."

example_sentences.japanese: わたしのなつやすみは、八日かんです。
example_sentences.english: My summer break is eight days long.

example_sentences.japanese: すみませんが、水を下さいませんか。もう八日もなにもたべていないんです。
example_sentences.english: Could you please give me some water? I haven't eaten anything for eight days.

example_sentences.japanese: らい月の八日にじの手じゅつをするよていです。
example_sentences.english: I’m going to get hemorrhoid surgery on the eighth of next month.

notes: "This vocab word has a weird little extra bit on it (the べ). You can sort of ignore that, it doesn't really mean anything in particular. The meaning of this vocab word and the kanji it comes from are the same: evening" When hiragana is attached to a kanji, you can usually assume that that kanji is going to be read using the kun'yomi reading, which is exactly what's going on with this word as well. By learning this word's kanji you've also learned the reading for this word.

example_sentences.japanese: 夕べ、パーティーにいきました。
example_sentences.english: I went to a party last night.

example_sentences.japanese: デンマークの王子はフランス人二人をおんがくの夕べにしょうたいしました。
example_sentences.english: The prince in Denmark invited two French people to a musical evening.

example_sentences.japanese: 夕べ、ひたいに肉とかいてみた。
example_sentences.english: Last night I wrote the kanji for meat on my forehead.

notes: "The mouth you exit out of is just a doorway (I hope), but an easier way to describe this word or concept is to call it an exit." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 出口 is an exception to this rule, however, and uses its kun'yomi readings. There's no particular reason why this is, but oftentimes a ""body part"" word (like mouth) changes a word to use kun'yomi readings instead of on'yomi ones. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 口 (くち) from learning the vocab, but to remember the reading for 出 you can think the following:If I exit out this mouth, I'll end up in the ocean (you were swallowed by a whale) and I will surely end up dead (で).Also keep in mind that because of rendaku, くち becomes ぐち."

example_sentences.japanese: そこは出口ではありません。
example_sentences.english: That is not an exit.

example_sentences.japanese: ふじ山にはひみつの入り口と出口があるらしいですよ。
example_sentences.english: I heard that Mt. Fuji has a secret entrance and exit.

example_sentences.japanese: このきゅうじょうの出口はあちらです。
example_sentences.english: This baseball stadium’s exit is over there.

notes: "What is an eye ball? Oh wait, that's easy. It's an eyeball!" "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 目玉, however, is an exception. Perhaps this is because it includes a body part (the eye) in it, which often makes a word switch to kun'yomi readings. Either way, it doesn't matter too much. Both the readings you learned for the kanji in this word are the kun'yomi, meaning you should know how to read this one. Just make sure you watch out for the rendaku."

example_sentences.japanese: このじゃがいもを、ゆきだるまの目玉にします。
example_sentences.english: I’ll use these potatoes for the snowman’s eyeballs.

example_sentences.japanese: 王女は目玉をコレクションするしゅみがあります。
example_sentences.english: The princess' hobby is to collect eyeballs.

example_sentences.japanese: ようかいの目玉のようなぶどうだとおもう。
example_sentences.english: I think these grapes look like monster eyeballs.

notes: "The kanji 月 means both month and moon (because moon cycles take about a month, presumably). So, what is the number two month? It's not January... it's not March... it's February!" "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That is true with this word as well. Make sure to take note that 月 is using the がつ reading and not the げつ one. This is true for all ""month words"" in Japanese."

example_sentences.japanese: 二月三日にけっこんしました。
example_sentences.english: I got married on February third.

example_sentences.japanese: 二月は、日本いきのチケットがとてもやすいです。
example_sentences.english: In February, air tickets to Japan are very cheap.

example_sentences.japanese: きょねんの二月に、わたしたちのふりんははじまったの。
example_sentences.english: Our affair began in February of last year.

english: Fifth Day, Day Five, Five Days
notes: "Day five or the fifth day. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense." "Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:On the fifth day I have to eat (いつ) five cars (か). Now imagine yourself eating five cars. How did you manage to get past the first one? I'm impressed."

example_sentences.japanese: 五日もしごとをやすみました。
example_sentences.english: I took five days off from work.

example_sentences.japanese: 六月五日はともだちのたんじょう日です。
example_sentences.english: June 5th is my friend's birthday.

example_sentences.japanese: 五日めに、「これでおしまい。」といった。
example_sentences.english: "On the fifth day I said, ""That's it!"""

notes: "What happens when you have ten five times? You get fifty!" This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That's the case for this word too, which means you should already know how to read this word.

example_sentences.japanese: かいてんずしで、五十さらたべた。
example_sentences.english: I ate fifty plates at conveyer belt sushi.

example_sentences.japanese: ある天才いしは、たったの五十えんでつうふうをなおすちりょうほうをはつめいしました。
example_sentences.english: One genius doctor invented a cure for gout for only 50 yen.

example_sentences.japanese: ほぼ五十ねんかんあなたのことがすきでしたが、きのうさめました。
example_sentences.english: I loved you for nearly fifty years, but yesterday that ended.

notes: "From previous number+つ words, you can probably guess that this word means five things." "The reading of this word is the kun'yomi reading of the kanji 五, meaning you didn't learn it when you learned the parent kanji reading. To remember this word, think of it this way:You have five things. What do you have to do with them? You need to eat (いつ) them. If you come up with something crazy you have to eat, and focus on the fact that you must eat five of these things, it will help a lot too."

example_sentences.japanese: わたしは五つもおもちをたべました。
example_sentences.english: I ate five pieces of mochi.

example_sentences.japanese: 五十人の白人のアメリカ人女子が、五つのおまんじゅうをてにいれようときそいあっています。
example_sentences.english: Fifty white female Americans are competing against each other to obtain five manju.

example_sentences.japanese: 人せいには五つのくるしみがあるが、その一つはへんずつうである。
example_sentences.english: There are five hardships in life and one of them is migraines.

notes: "A genius from heaven is still a genius." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. As long as you know the readings for these kanji, you should be able to read this word just fine.

example_sentences.japanese: かれはしょうぎの天才です。
example_sentences.english: He’s a shogi genius.

example_sentences.japanese: あのフランス人の女は天才だ。
example_sentences.english: That French woman is genius.

example_sentences.japanese: そのゴリラは、まぎれもなく天才だ。
example_sentences.english: That gorilla is definitely a genius.

notes: "Since the kanji 月 mean both moon and month (because a moon cycle is about a month, presumably), what is the number one month? In English we have an actual name for it, and that name is January." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. This is a specific month, so it uses the がつ reading."

example_sentences.japanese: わたしは一月にかんじを千こおぼえました。
example_sentences.english: I learned one thousand kanji in January.

example_sentences.japanese: 一月うまれのアメリカ人と六月うまれのイタリア人では、どちらのほうがおおいとおもいますか。
example_sentences.english: Which do you think there are more of: Americans who were born in January or Italians who were born in June?

example_sentences.japanese: 一月にたべるアイスクリームもわるくない。
example_sentences.english: It’s not bad to eat ice cream in January.

notes: "Remember the secondary meaning of 本? It's ""origin."" So, this word technically means ""sun origin."" Does that sound familiar? Japan's known as ""The land of the rising sun."" That's why Japan comes from 日本." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well, though take note that the 日 portion is shortened a bit. So instead of being にち it is just に."

example_sentences.japanese: 日本のカレーはおいしいです。
example_sentences.english: Japanese curry is delicious.

example_sentences.japanese: 十月から、日本にすみます。
example_sentences.english: I'm gonna live in Japan starting in October.

example_sentences.japanese: 日本のかたちをしたケーキをやいた。
example_sentences.english: I baked a cake shaped like Japan.

notes: "Since the kanji 月 means both ""moon"" and ""month,"" what is the sixth month of the year? January, February, March, April, May, June!" "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Also, this is a specific month, so it uses the がつ reading."

example_sentences.japanese: 六月にとうきょうへいきました。
example_sentences.english: I went to Tokyo in June.

example_sentences.japanese: 五月に刀を二本かって、六月にトーフグのオフィスでつじぎりをします。
example_sentences.english: I will buy two katanas in May and test them at the Tofugu office in June.

example_sentences.japanese: 六月のてんきは、くもりときどきミートボールです。
example_sentences.english: The weather for June is cloudy with a chance of meatballs.

notes: "The moon kanji also represents a month, so when you have five of these months, what month of the year is it? That would be May, the greatest month of the year (because it has towel day in it!)." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Also, this is a specific month, so it uses the がつ reading."

example_sentences.japanese: 五月四日にくにへかえりました。
example_sentences.english: I went back to my country on May fourth.

example_sentences.japanese: 五月にはゴールデンウィークがあります。
example_sentences.english: Golden week is in May.

example_sentences.japanese: 五月に川へいきます。
example_sentences.english: I’m going to a river in May.

english: Nine Days, Day Nine, Ninth Day
notes: "Ninth day or day nine. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense." "Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both of the kanji. You learned this reading for 九 when you learned 九つ, so you should be able to read this one too!"

example_sentences.japanese: 九日に、いっしょにサッカーをみにいきませんか。
example_sentences.english: Would you like to go watch some soccer with me on the ninth?

example_sentences.japanese: コウイチは九日もニッカにあっていないので、さびしくてしにそうだ。
example_sentences.english: Since Koichi hasn't seen Nikka for nine days, he feels so lonely he could die.

example_sentences.japanese: マミのたんじょう日は四がつ九日だ。
example_sentences.english: Mami’s birthday is April ninth.

notes: "The kanji for ""moon"" and ""month"" are the same, probably because a moon cycle takes approximately a month to occur. So, what is the tenth moon cycle of the year? That would be the awesome month October!" "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.Also, this is a specific month, so it uses the がつ reading."

example_sentences.japanese: さらいねんの十月で、六十さいになります。
example_sentences.english: Two years from now I will turn sixty in October.

example_sentences.japanese: 十月にはだんだんすずしくなってくるでしょう。
example_sentences.english: It should gradually be getting cooler in October.

example_sentences.japanese: かれがおかしいのは、十月なのにすいえいにさそったわたしのせきにんだ。
example_sentences.english: It’s my fault that he’s acting strange; I asked him to go swimming even though it is October.

hiragana: いちにち, ついたち
english: One Day, Day One, First Day
notes: "This word has two different meanings. One day and first day. No matter how you look at this word, those meanings make a lot of sense." "The first meaning is one day, and it has the same reading as the kanji you learned, so you should already know this reading.The reading for first day, however, is a big old exception. It doesn’t take the on’yomi or kun’yomi readings, and has its own special (weird) readings. Here’s a mnemonic to help  you remember this one:On the first day of your new relationship you can get two touches (ついたち) only. That’s the rule! You can touch their hand and maybe high five. But that’s all you get. Just think when you’re on your first day of dating, two touches! Two touches only!"

example_sentences.japanese: きのうは一日テストのべんきょうをしていました。
example_sentences.english: I was studying for the test all day yesterday.

example_sentences.japanese: 六月一日にアメリカ人とフランス人のふうふ二人がいっしょにエベレストをのぼりきったことは人々のきおくにあたらしい。
example_sentences.english: The fact that an American and French couple succeeded to climb Mt. Everest on June 1st is still fresh in people's memory.

example_sentences.japanese: 本とうに一日でこの本をよんだんですか？
example_sentences.english: Did you really read this book in one day?

notes: "If you have one thousand, you have one thousand." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The only thing that's a bit weird is the reading of the 一. The ち turns into a small っ, making the reading for this word いっせん."

example_sentences.japanese: そのライブには、一千まん人があつまった。
example_sentences.english: Ten million people gathered at the live show.

example_sentences.japanese: その刀は、一千えんです。
example_sentences.english: That katana is one thousand yen.

example_sentences.japanese: 一千フィートのたかさでおならをした。
example_sentences.english: I farted at an elevation of 1000 feet.

english: One Thousand Yen, A Thousand Yen, Thousand Yen
notes: "A thousand of these yen things makes this word one thousand yen." Since you know the on'yomi readings of these two kanji, you should know the reading for this vocab word as well!

example_sentences.japanese: このスカートは、千円です。
example_sentences.english: This skirt is 1000 yen.

example_sentences.japanese: ぎゅうにゅうのねだんが千円上がった。
example_sentences.english: The price of milk rose by 1000 yen.

example_sentences.japanese: あのやきゅうせんしゅのねんぽうは五千円だ。
example_sentences.english: That baseball player makes 5,000 yen per year.

notes: "A child dog is a puppy!" "Even though this is a jukugo word, it doesn't use the on'yomi readings. Both the kanji 子 and 犬 often favor kun'yomi readings, and this word is no exception. The reading for 犬 is the one you already know, and the reading for 子 as こ is a really common one (perhaps you've already learned that reading?). If not, just think about punching a puppy in the face, and giving it a KO (That's a knock out)."

example_sentences.japanese: けさ、子犬がうまれました。
example_sentences.english: The puppies were born this morning.

example_sentences.japanese: その子犬は王子にもらった九つの玉をくびから下げて入り口に立っていた。
example_sentences.english: The puppy that was standing at the entrance was given the nine balls around its neck by the prince.

example_sentences.japanese: 子犬ごっこをしましょうよ。
example_sentences.english: Let’s pretend we’re puppies!

english: Second Day, Day Two, Two Days
notes: "Second day or day two. No matter how you look at this combination of kanji, the meaning of the word makes a lot of sense!" "Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:The circus is in town this weekend and you can't wait to get there. You want to show off your new foots car (ふつか) to all the circus clowns. But you have to use your feet to get it there and it ends up taking you two days! Darn this old fashioned foots car!"

example_sentences.japanese: らい月の二日に、あねとえいがをみにいきます。
example_sentences.english: I will go see a movie with my older sister on the second day of next month.

example_sentences.japanese: 王子が子犬をおってふじ山のじゅかいにきえてから二日がたちました。
example_sentences.english: It's been two days since the prince followed the puppy and disappeared in the woods of Mt. Fuji.

example_sentences.japanese: ひらがななんて、しんけんにべんきょうすれば二日あれば十ぶんさ。
example_sentences.english: If you study diligently, two days is enough to learn hiragana.

english: Seventh Day, Day Seven, Seven Days
notes: "Seventh day or day seven. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense." "Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:You've been stuck inside working for seven days and today you finally have a day off. Your friend asks you if you want to go for a drive but you say, ""Nah, no car today"" (なのか), because you've been cooped up long enough. Seven days is too long to be inside."

example_sentences.japanese: かぜで、七日かんもねこんでいました。
example_sentences.english: I was in bed for seven whole days because of a cold.

example_sentences.japanese: まい月七日に、おはかまいりをします。
example_sentences.english: I visit our family grave on the 7th of every month.

example_sentences.japanese: たった七日でかいしゃをやめた。
example_sentences.english: I left the company after only seven days.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. Numbers, as you know, are the exception to this rule. They usually use the on'yomi reading, and the on'yomi reading is the one you learned along with this kanji, meaning you should be good to go!

example_sentences.japanese: 山本さんのでんわばんごうは、六一二の七七三六ですね？
example_sentences.english: Is Yamamoto’s phone number 612-7736?

example_sentences.japanese: 六じにふじ山であいましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's meet at Mt. Fuji at six o'clock.

example_sentences.japanese: 六かける六は三十六ですよね？
example_sentences.english: Six times six is thirty-six, right?

notes: "You have ten and six (not to be confused with six tens!). When you have ten and six, you have a total of sixteen." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well!

example_sentences.japanese: 十六さいのたんじょうびにふじ山にのぼりました。
example_sentences.english: I climbed Mt. Fuji on my sixteenth birthday.

example_sentences.japanese: もう十六ねんもふじ山の入り口からうごかないアメリカ人がいます。
example_sentences.english: There is an American who hasn't moved away from the entrance of Mt. Fuji for 16 years.

example_sentences.japanese: わたしはえいえんの十六さいです。
example_sentences.english: I am forever sixteen.

english: Sixth Day, Day Six, Six Days
notes: "It's the kanji for six and day. Put them together and you have the sixth day (or day six)." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. This is an exception, though. When you're counting days (at least one through ten), the kun'yomi readings are used. So let's think about that sixth day - what does it entail?The cow (moo / むい) is standing on top of your car (か). Why? Because you only feed the cow once a week, and that is on the seventh day. He's standing there on the sixth day because he's super hungry and knows it's almost time."

example_sentences.japanese: 二人は、せん月の六日に、どこであいましたか？
example_sentences.english: Where did you two meet on the sixth of last month?

example_sentences.japanese: 六日もがっこうをやすんで、いったいなにをしてたんだい？
example_sentences.english: What were you doing when you took six days off of school?

example_sentences.japanese: 月の六日目に、くまがバーにやってきた。
example_sentences.english: A bear came into the bar on the sixth day of the month.

notes: "Any number with a つ attached to it means you are counting that number of things. In this case, it's six things." "Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can guess that it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you do that:What are the six things that you need to count? This time you are counting six cows (むっつ). The reason it's six, you know, is because you wanted a half a dozen cows. No more, no less."

example_sentences.japanese: わたしのへやには、テーブルが一つと、いすが六つあります。
example_sentences.english: In my room, there is one table and six chairs.

example_sentences.japanese: 川から石を六つもってかえりました。
example_sentences.english: I brought back six stones from the river.

example_sentences.japanese: わたしは、六つのカップをかいました。
example_sentences.english: I bought six packs of cups.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. "Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: You look through the soil. You're trying to find something. As you dig and sift, you come across not one but two cheeses (つち). Pull them out of the ground and put them in your mouth. How do the two cheeses taste and compare?"

example_sentences.japanese: これは、こうしえんの土です。
example_sentences.english: This is Koshien’s dirt.

example_sentences.japanese: このビー玉を七つ土にうめたら、天のこえがきこえます。
example_sentences.english: If you bury seven of these marbles, you will hear the voice of heaven.

example_sentences.japanese: マットのしゅみは、土をほりあげることだ。
example_sentences.english: Matt’s hobby is digging dirt.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well! "Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. I'm hoping you already know this word - that will make everything much easier. It's かたな (you know what a katana is, right?)."

example_sentences.japanese: あのさむらいに、刀をぬすまれたんだ。
example_sentences.english: My sword was stolen by that samurai.

example_sentences.japanese: あのアメリカ人は刀を二ほんもっている。
example_sentences.english: That American has two katanas.

example_sentences.japanese: スラリと刀をぬいたあのおとこはだれだ？
example_sentences.english: Who’s the guy who just whipped out a sword?

english: Ten Days, Day Ten, Tenth Day
notes: "Tenth day or day ten. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense." "Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:Ten days is just TOO (とお) long from now. Maybe less would have been okay, but ten is too much."

example_sentences.japanese: このくすりを、十日かんのんでください。
example_sentences.english: Please take this medicine for ten days.

example_sentences.japanese: 十日でかんせいさせてください。
example_sentences.english: Please complete it within ten days.

example_sentences.japanese: 七月十日はそふのめい日です。
example_sentences.english: The tenth of July is the anniversary of my grandfather’s death.

english: Third Day, Day Three, Three Days
notes: "Third day or day three. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Counting days, however, are an exception (at least up to ten). You need to use the kun'yomi readings to read this word. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 三 from when you learned the word 三つ. Here is a way to remember the reading for 日:On the third day you have to give me (み) a ride in your car (か). I don't have a car of my own, so don't forget me, okay?"

example_sentences.japanese: 二人は、せんせん月の三日にどこであいましたか？
example_sentences.english: Where did those two people meet on the third, two months ago?

example_sentences.japanese: 三日も水をのんでいません。
example_sentences.english: I haven't had water for three days.

example_sentences.japanese: 三月三日はひなまつりです。
example_sentences.english: The third day of March is Girl’s Day.

notes: "A fire mountain is probably what you think it is: A volcano." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The 山 reading is ざん instead of さん because of rendaku (sequential voicing)."

example_sentences.japanese: 火山のふんかもありました。
example_sentences.english: There was a volcanic eruption too.

example_sentences.japanese: ふじ山は火山です。いまから四十二じかんごにふんかします。
example_sentences.english: Mt. Fuji is a volcano. It will erupt in 42 hours.

example_sentences.japanese: きっと火山にちがいない。
example_sentences.english: I’m sure that’s a volcano.

hiragana: あめりかじん, アメリカじん
notes: "The アメリカ part is pretty easy so long as you know katakana. It's the word for ""America."" You know that 人 means ""person,"" so you can figure out that America + Person = American." "Often times when two kanji come together to form a combo kanji you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. So, the reading of 人 is the on'yomi reading じん, which you learned already in the kanji. This pattern works with almost any location as well. Just add a country name + 人 and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here."

example_sentences.japanese: おれはアメリカ人か？
example_sentences.english: Am I American?

example_sentences.japanese: アメリカ人が二人います。
example_sentences.english: There are two American people.

example_sentences.japanese: アメリカ人の女とともだちになった。
example_sentences.english: I made friends with an American girl.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

example_sentences.japanese: 矢はなん本のこっていますか？
example_sentences.english: How many arrows are left?

example_sentences.japanese: こいのキューピッドが矢をはなとうとしているよ。
example_sentences.english: Cupid is about to fire an arrow.

example_sentences.japanese: ほくべい土人の矢じりがとんできた。
example_sentences.english: A Native American arrowhead flew towards me.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. "Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: You're leading the cows around the field. To get them to move, you yell out ""USH, USH, USH!"" (うし) because you have a speech impediment and want to say ""MUSH MUSH MUSH."" Go ahead and say this out loud, yelling it if you can."

example_sentences.japanese: しゃちょうは牛をかっているらしい。
example_sentences.english: Apparently the company president is raising a cow.

example_sentences.japanese: かの女は、牛がらのドレスをきて、牛どんやに行ってきました。
example_sentences.english: She came to a gyudon restaurant in a cow-spot patterned dress.

example_sentences.japanese: デイブは、牛にゅうのために牛をかっている。
example_sentences.english: Dave keeps cows for milk.

notes: "Do you remember the words 出口 (exit) and 入り口 (entrance) from previous levels? The 口 can be a doorway of some kind. This word is literally ""door mouth"" but I bet you can figure out that this actually means doorway." "The reading for this one is mixed. You get the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, even though it's a combo (jukugo) kanji. Since 戸's only reading is the kun'yomi reading you should know it. Also, you should know the kun'yomi reading for 口 as well from level 1. That means as long as you remember that this is a kun'yomi fest over here, you should be able to read this word. Also watch out for the rendaku (also known as sequential voicing). That just means the く becomes the voiced ぐ."

example_sentences.japanese: 戸口に手ぶくろがおちていました。
example_sentences.english: A glove was dropped in the doorway.

example_sentences.japanese: たまたま、戸口でぬすみぎきしてしまったんです。
example_sentences.english: I  eavesdropped it at the doorway by accident.

example_sentences.japanese: 戸口に三枚のトーストがあった。
example_sentences.english: There were three pieces of toast in my doorway.

notes: "As long as you know both of the individual kanji meanings, you should be able to put together this one to get five machines." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: たいじゅうけいを五台かいました。
example_sentences.english: I bought five scales.

example_sentences.japanese: あのいえのまえに、パトカーが五台もとまっている。
example_sentences.english: There are five police cars parked in front of that house.

example_sentences.japanese: 五台のバンがげきとつしてめりこんだ。
example_sentences.english: The five vans smashed into each other.

notes: "An ""outside person"" is a foreigner. This word is fairly common, though it's not super polite, either. It's okay most of the time, but it can be used derogatorily depending on the situation. The more polite version is 外国人 (outside country person) but you won't learn that until you learn the kanji for 国." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, you can remember that for this word it uses じん because foreigners like to wear jeans (じん)."

example_sentences.japanese: 田中さんのむすめさんは外人さんとけっこんしたんだよ。
example_sentences.english: Tanaka’s daughter got married to a foreigner.

example_sentences.japanese: でんしゃでよっぱらった外人にからまれた。
example_sentences.english: A drunk foreigner tried to pick a fight with me on the train.

example_sentences.japanese: 日本人と外人のあしのながさはかなりちがう。
example_sentences.english: Leg length is quite different between Japanese people and foreigners.

hiragana: ふらんすじん, フランスじん
notes: "フランス is ""France."" So what is a ""France person?"" That would be a French Person." "You can treat this word and the 人 kanji on the end like jukugo (combo kanji). Usually, in the case of jukugo, you use the on'yomi reading. So here you'll want to remember to use the on'yomi reading for 人. If you want, you can add 人 to the end of any place name to describe the people that live there!"

example_sentences.japanese: フランス人のゆうじんができました。
example_sentences.english: I made a French friend.

example_sentences.japanese: 二人はアメリカ人で、あとの三人はフランス人です。
example_sentences.english: Two of them are American and the other three are French.

example_sentences.japanese: とてもセクシーなフランス人シェフにあった。
example_sentences.english: I met a very sexy French chef.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. "Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Look down! You're wearing something covered in fur. It's a fur kevlar (け) vest! All kevlar is just really tightly woven fur. Didn't you know?"

example_sentences.japanese: あしの毛がボーボーです。
example_sentences.english: My leg hair is bushy.

example_sentences.japanese: うちの犬の毛はよくぬける。
example_sentences.english: Our dog's fur falls off a lot.

example_sentences.japanese: 今一ばん大切なのはあたまの毛だ。
example_sentences.english: Right now the most important thing to me is the hair on my head.

notes: "A public task is going to be government business. You have to think of this public as government to know the meaning of this word easily." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 今、公用でパリにきています。
example_sentences.english: I’m coming to Paris now on official business.

example_sentences.japanese: これは公用のアカウントです。
example_sentences.english: This is an official account.

example_sentences.japanese: おれたちがぬすむのは公用のかねだ。
example_sentences.english: We’re gonna steal government money.

notes:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

"How much can you hold in this ladle? Why, exactly eighteen liters of course! Eighteen is your favorite number, how convenient." The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

example_sentences.japanese: 戸をたたかないでください。
example_sentences.english: Please don’t knock on the door.

example_sentences.japanese: うちのねこは戸をカリカリするのがすきです。
example_sentences.english: My cat likes scratching the door.

example_sentences.japanese: この戸は立てつけがわるい。
example_sentences.english: This door opens and closes hard.

example_sentences.japanese: 一斗のお米が入った袋は置いてますか？
example_sentences.english: Do you have a bag of 18 liters of rice?

hiragana: びーだま, ビーだま
notes: "Presumably this ビー is short for the word ""bead."" Beads used to be glass, which means that if you have a glass bead ball, you probably have yourself a marble." "If you know katakana as well as the reading that you learned when you learned the kanji 玉, you should be able to read this. Just watch out for the rendaku."

example_sentences.japanese: ビー玉をつかってゲームをしましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let’s play a game that uses marbles.

example_sentences.japanese: アメリカではまいとし一月にビー玉をつかったゲームが上手なフランス人がつどうコンテストがあります。
example_sentences.english: In America, there is a contest every January where French people who are good at marbles gather.

example_sentences.japanese: かれは、けっこんのあかしに一つぶのビー玉をくれた。
example_sentences.english: He gave me a single marble as proof of our marriage.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. "Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You're going to the far north where it's very cold (north pole, perhaps?). One of the most important things you bring with you is a survival kit (きた)."

example_sentences.japanese: えきの北には、びょういんがあります。
example_sentences.english: There is a hospital on the north side of the station.

example_sentences.japanese: 北ちょうせんが又ミサイルをはっしゃした。
example_sentences.english: North Korea launched a missile again.

example_sentences.japanese: 北アメリカのゆうれいはとてもこわい。
example_sentences.english: The ghosts in North America are so scary.

notes:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. "Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: What'll you drink now? I'll have a Zima, ima.Say ""ZIMA IMA"" ten times fast."

"A room that comes alive in intervals is your living room. You don't spend all your time in there, so it can only be alive sometimes. This word is usually used for western style living rooms by the way, so don't mistake it for a traditional Japanese one." The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

example_sentences.japanese: 今、しんぶんをよんでいます。
example_sentences.english: I’m reading the newspaper right now.

example_sentences.japanese: おれは今までなにをしていたんだ。
example_sentences.english: What was I doing until now?

example_sentences.japanese: 今から、ヘルメットにおはようといいます。
example_sentences.english: Now I’m going to say good morning to my helmet.

example_sentences.japanese: 父は居間でテレビを観ています。
example_sentences.english: Dad is watching TV in the living room.

english: Number Of People, People, People Counter, Counter For People
notes: "When you see this on a number, for example ７人 or ３人, you're using it to count people. Just remember, both 一人 and 二人 have alternative readings. From 3 and up it's just the number plus にん, like this. ５人 is ごにん, １０人 is じゅうにん, etc. This is the counter for people, which makes this word the number of people." "The reading is the にん reading of this kanji. Just think of a number of people, all ninjas, standing there as you count them out."

example_sentences.japanese: ぜんぶで十人いました。
example_sentences.english: There were 10 people, altogether.

example_sentences.japanese: トーフグにはなん人のしゃいんがいますか？
example_sentences.english: How many workers are in Tofugu?

example_sentences.japanese: わたしは三人子どもがいます。
example_sentences.english: I have three children.

english: One Hundred Thousand, Hundred Thousand, A Hundred Thousand
notes: "Ten ten thousands is equal to one hundred thousand." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: パチンコで十万円かちました。
example_sentences.english: I won one hundred thousand yen at pachinko.

example_sentences.japanese: このアイフォンは、十万六千九ひゃく円でした。
example_sentences.english: This iPhone cost me 106,900 yen.

example_sentences.japanese: ウォッカをのむと、すう十万でん子ボルトものエネルギーがみなぎってくる。
example_sentences.english: Whenever I drink vodka, I get pumped full of hundreds of thousands of electron volts.

notes:
As long as you know the two kanji that make up this word, you should be able to figure out the meaning of this word as well. This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

"This word has the kanji for one and period. You only have one period to live in so this is the only lifetime you get. Unless you're reborn, but that will probably be in the next age, not this one. So one lifetime for you!" This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: このテレビは、一台四万九千円です。
example_sentences.english: These televisions are forty-nine thousand yen each.

example_sentences.japanese: 今はパソコン一台でかせぐじだいですからね。
example_sentences.english: We're living in an era where you can make a living with a single computer.

example_sentences.japanese: タクシーを一台よんでください。
example_sentences.english: Could you call me a taxi?

example_sentences.japanese: かれは、一代でここまでかいしゃを大きくした。
example_sentences.english: He made the company this much larger in just one generation.

example_sentences.japanese: コウイチは一世一代の大しょうぶに打って出た。
example_sentences.english: Koichi went to take a once-in-a-lifetime gamble.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は一代で巨額の財産を作ったが、彼の息子がさらにそれを二倍にした。
example_sentences.english: He amassed an enormous fortune over the course of his lifetime and his son doubled it.

notes:
"The kanji for person and life combined makes you think about human life. What is your human life like?" This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

"A person's nature is just human nature! Everyone has their own human instincts." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 人生ってすばらしい。
example_sentences.english: Life is wonderful.

example_sentences.japanese: 人生オワタ ＼(＾o＾)／
example_sentences.english: My life is over. ＼(＾o＾)／

example_sentences.japanese: 人生はバナナのようなものさ。どれだけながいのかだれもしらないのさ。
example_sentences.english: Life is like a banana, you never know how long it will be.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は、大学で人性学を勉強しています。
example_sentences.english: I'm learning ethology at university.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は、キリストは神性と人性という二つの本性を持つという両性せつを支持します。
example_sentences.english: I support the dyophysite that Jesus has two natures: a divine nature and a human nature.

example_sentences.japanese: 人性論における人間の本性において、私は結局人の性質は善悪を共に備えていると思います。
example_sentences.english: With regard to the discussion about original human nature in Confucianism, I believe that human nature is equipped with both good and evil sides after all.

hiragana: しあとるし, シアトルし
notes: "The name of the city (シアトル／しあとる) with a 市 attached to it means it is ""the city of ____."" You can do this with any city (try it out on your hometown!). Because of this, you should know that this word means Seattle, or more specifically City of Seattle." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 今はシアトル市にすんでいます。
example_sentences.english: I live in Seattle now.

example_sentences.japanese: わたしのお母さんは、シアトル市でそだちました。
example_sentences.english: My mother grew up in Seattle.

example_sentences.japanese: あなたのへんがおしゃしんを、シアトル市におくります。
example_sentences.english: I will send that funny picture of you to Seattle.

notes: If you know the two kanji separately, you should be able to put them together to form the meaning of this kanji. This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: パソコンを十台ちゅう文しました。
example_sentences.english: We ordered ten computers.

example_sentences.japanese: ぼうはんカメラを十台せっちしました。
example_sentences.english: We installed ten surveillance cameras.

example_sentences.japanese: たんじょう日にはでんたくが十台ほしい。
example_sentences.english: I want ten calculators for my birthday.

notes: "When you have one ten thousand you just have ten thousand. In Japanese, though, you specify how many ten thousands you have, though (which is weird in English, but should make sense if you think about it)." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: わたしのぜんざいさんは一万円です。
example_sentences.english: Ten thousand yen is all I have.

example_sentences.japanese: 一万RTいったら、こく白します。
example_sentences.english: If this gets ten thousand retweets, I'll confess my love.

example_sentences.japanese: ちくしょう！にせの一万円さつをつかまされた。
example_sentences.english: Crap! I was cheated into accepting a fake 10,000 yen bill.

notes: "When a vocab word is a single kanji without okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it usually has the same meaning as the kanji it's spawned from. If you know the kanji meaning you'll also know the vocab meaning. It's ten thousand!" When a vocab word is a single kanji with no okurigana, it usually uses the kun'yomi reading. Numbers are an exception to this. Numbers use the on'yomi reading, which you've already learned by learning the kanji's reading! How nice!

example_sentences.japanese: 日本へのひこうきだいは、十万五千円でした。
example_sentences.english: The plane ticket to Japan cost 105,000 yen.

example_sentences.japanese: まいとしコウイチは、バレンタインデーに万たんいのチョコレートをもらいます。
example_sentences.english: Every year Koichi receives tens of thousands of chocolates on Valentine's Day.

example_sentences.japanese: ごしゅうぎのそうばは大たい三万円です。
example_sentences.english: The estimate on a congratulatory gift is approximately 30,000 yen.

notes: "The now month is actually this month." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 今月は大じなしけんがあります。
example_sentences.english: There is an important exam this month.

example_sentences.japanese: おそくとも、今月の中じゅんまでにかんせいさせてください。
example_sentences.english: Please complete this by the middle of this month, at the latest.

example_sentences.japanese: 今月は、ちょうのちょう子があまりよくない。
example_sentences.english: My stomach hasn’t been feeling well this month.

notes: "The now day is what day? Oh, it's today." "The reading for this word is a complete exception, though the word itself is incredibly common and useful. When you think of ""today"" think about what you have to do today for work.You have to work in one of those mall kiosks (きょう). Just think about how sad you are that you have to do this today. What a crummy day. It's sunny outside and you're stuck in a mall manning this hermit crab kiosk.Note: This reading mnemonic is pretty far away from the actual reading, as far as reading mnemonics go. Use this to get yourself close, and then use your own brain grapes to get the rest of the way there. This one won't be as easy as most of the others, but do some good old fashioned memorization and you should be okay. I won't ask you to do this much, fortunately. :)"

example_sentences.japanese: 今日のしゅくだいは、二十一ページの二ばんです。
example_sentences.english: Today’s homework is question two on page twenty-one.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日はいつもよりうり上げが少ない。
example_sentences.english: Today's sales are less than usual.

example_sentences.japanese: あら、今日が私のたん生日だったんですか？
example_sentences.english: Oh, was today my birthday?

notes: "When you have two ten thousands, you have twenty thousand." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: このぶどうは二万円もしました。
example_sentences.english: These grapes were 20,000 yen!

example_sentences.japanese: 二万フォロワーおめでとうございます。
example_sentences.english: Congratulations on twenty thousand followers!

example_sentences.japanese: 二万ドルかけるよ。
example_sentences.english: I will bet twenty thousand dollars.

notes: "When you combine these two kanji, you should be able to see how it forms the word two machines." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: どうしてけいたいを二台もっているんですか。
example_sentences.english: Why do you have two cell phones?

example_sentences.japanese: コウイチの母のいえには、ピアノが二台ある。
example_sentences.english: There are two pianos at Koichi's mom's house.

example_sentences.japanese: うちのトイレにはテレビが二台しかない。
example_sentences.english: There are only two televisions in our bathroom.

notes: "The の particle makes it so the 人 belongs to the 女. Basically, this literally means ""a woman person"" or ""a person of woman."" It's a more polite way to say plain old woman, though, so all you have to remember is that." This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). That being said, in level 1 you learned about the vocab readings for these separate words, so use that knowledge to remember the reading for this word as well.

example_sentences.japanese: わたしは女の人にいじめられた。
example_sentences.english: I was bullied by a woman.

example_sentences.japanese: そのカフェは女の人だらけでした。
example_sentences.english: The cafe was full of women.

example_sentences.japanese: 女の人としゃべるのが苦手です。
example_sentences.english: I’m not good at talking to women.

notes: "If there is a big energy it's going to fill up the atmosphere! Think about big energies you feel in the atmosphere: thunderstorms, tornadoes, the aurora borealis. Just remember, this is the atmosphere in the sky, not the atmosphere in a fancy restaurant." This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

example_sentences.japanese: 大気おせんマップを毎日チェックしています。
example_sentences.english: I check the atmospheric pollution map everyday.

example_sentences.japanese: そらがあおいのは、ちきゅうの大気の分子があおとみどりのひかりをさんらんするからです。
example_sentences.english: The sky is blue because blue and green lights are scattered in all directions by the air molecules in Earth's atmosphere.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日も、ぜんこく的に大気のじょうたいがふあんていです。
example_sentences.english: Air conditions are unstable nationwide again today.

notes:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well! Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading which is also the reading you associated with the kanji, earlier.

"The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This word is usually used for clothing height and length." "The reading is different from what you learned with the kanji. Remember the word 竹? It has the same reading as this. Just think of everyone measuring the heights of things with bamboo (たけ) poles with markers on them. Okay, this one is 5 bamboo poles high!"

example_sentences.japanese: このおはしは竹でできています。
example_sentences.english: These chopsticks are made of bamboo.

example_sentences.japanese: 竹は、一メートルぐらいのたかさまで切ってしまうと、ねまでかれてしまいます。
example_sentences.english: If you cut a bamboo to about a meter high, it dies and even its roots wither.

example_sentences.japanese: 竹細工が本当に好きなんだ！うちのテレビも俺が竹から作ったんだよ。まあ、動かないけどね。でも、見た目がいいんだよ。
example_sentences.english: I love working with bamboo! I made my television out of bamboo. It doesn’t work, but it sure looks nice.

example_sentences.japanese: ユニクロで、七分丈のパンツを買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a pair of three-quarter-length pants at UNIQLO.

example_sentences.japanese: 少し見ないうちに、ずいぶん丈がのびたな！
example_sentences.english: You've grown a lot taller since I saw you last!

example_sentences.japanese: 話を変える訳じゃないんだけど、そのスカートはちょっと丈が長過ぎるんじゃないかしら？
example_sentences.english: Not to change the subject, but isn’t that skirt just a little too long for you?

notes: "What is a child of bamboo? That would be a baby bamboo. Because ""baby bamboo"" doesn't really make sense, we'll instead call this word bamboo shoots. P.S. Fresh bamboo shoots cooked on a fire are delicious, make sure you try them sometime." "If you know the readings of the kanji for 竹 and the vocabulary for 子 you should be able to read this word as well."

example_sentences.japanese: 竹の子をゆでているところです。
example_sentences.english: I’m boiling bamboo shoots.

example_sentences.japanese: ふじ山の入り口から北の方にのぼっていくと、と中に竹の子が山のようにとれるところがあります。
example_sentences.english: If you go up north from the entrance of Mt. Fuji, there is a place where you can dig up a lot of bamboo shoots on your way.

example_sentences.japanese: 「あ、お兄さん。わかりました。わかりました。竹の子、好きなだけ持って行ってください。」とパンダが言った。
example_sentences.english: """Hey, man. It’s cool, it’s cool. Take all the bamboo shoots you want,"" said the panda."

notes:
"You have a child cow. What do you think a child cow is? Probably a calf or a baby cow." "Since you should know the readings of the words 子 and 牛 from the previous level, you should be able to read this word too even though it's using the kun'yomi readings for the kanji."

"A lecture expert is a lecturer or instructor." This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

example_sentences.japanese: 白い子牛をかっているんです。
example_sentences.english: We have a white calf.

example_sentences.japanese: この子牛は、とても元気です。
example_sentences.english: This calf is very energetic.

example_sentences.japanese: お父さん！サンタ・クロースが昨夜子牛をくれたわ！
example_sentences.english: Daddy! Santa Claus gave me a calf last night!

example_sentences.japanese: その大学の講師としての資格を得ました。
example_sentences.english: I qualified as a lecturer for the university.

notes: "The flower fire... what looks like flowers on fire? That would be fireworks. Totally makes sense, right?" "The readings for the kanji that make this word are the kun'yomi readings, where fire's ひ changes to び. You already learned the kun'yomi reading for 花 when you learned the kanji, so it's only a matter of remembering to use the kun'yomi for 火. If you do, you should be able to read this word."

example_sentences.japanese: 花火が上がるのはきんよう日だけです。
example_sentences.english: The fireworks are only going off on Friday.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、かぞくで花火大かいに出かけました。
example_sentences.english: I went to see a fireworks display with my family yesterday.

example_sentences.japanese: 花火ってめっちゃいい匂いだよね？
example_sentences.english: Fireworks have a great smell, don’t they?

notes: "You'd maybe think this just means one year of life, but it actually means first year student. A second year student is a 二年生, and so on. Just think about how crazy the Japanese are about school. You can see why school is life, and not life itself, making this vocab word ""first year student.""" This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 川下さんは、小がく一年生のおとうとがいます。
example_sentences.english: Kawashita has a brother who is a first year student in elementary school.

example_sentences.japanese: ことしの四月、わたしは中がく一年生になり、わたしのいもうとは小学一年生、兄はこうこう一年生、母と父は大学一年生になります。
example_sentences.english: This April, I’m starting the first year of middle school, my little sister is starting the first year of elementary school, my older brother is starting the first year of high school, and my mother and father are starting the first year of university.

example_sentences.japanese: まだ小学一年生が学ぶ漢字ですら知りません。
example_sentences.english: I haven’t even learned the kanji that first grade elementary school students know yet.

notes: "When you have five hundreds you also have five hundred." This word uses the on'yomi readings for both kanji, so you should be able to read it already!

example_sentences.japanese: 三月まつまでに、かん字を五百こおぼえてください。
example_sentences.english: Please memorize five hundred kanji by the end of March.

example_sentences.japanese: 日本には五百円玉というものがあります。
example_sentences.english: Japan has 500-yen coins.

example_sentences.japanese: 「どうやって五百頭もの馬を車に乗せるっていうの？」と女が聞いた。「そうだよね。代わりにバンを持ってきた方が良かったかな。」と男は答えた。
example_sentences.english: """How are we going to get five hundred horses into one car?"" asked the woman. ""You’re right! Do you think I should have bought the van instead?"" the man replied."

notes:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. This is the reading you learned when you learned the kanji, so you're good to go. Don't forget to stop and smell the roses on the way, though.

The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. The reading is the same as the kanji. Smells nice, right?

example_sentences.japanese: ヒマワリは、とてもきれいな花です。
example_sentences.english: The sunflower is a very beautiful flower.

example_sentences.japanese: この花の花ことばは、はな毛ボーボーです。
example_sentences.english: In the language of flowers, this one means bushy nose hair.

example_sentences.japanese: 何か花を使った料理が知りたいんだけど。花のスープとかって聞いたことある？
example_sentences.english: I want to learn how to cook with flowers. Have you ever heard of flower soup?

example_sentences.japanese: ぼくの鼻のことにはふれずに、そっとしておいてくれませんか？
example_sentences.english: Could you stop poking my nose and leave me alone?

example_sentences.japanese: 鼻をほじると、鼻のあなは大きくなりますか？
example_sentences.english: Can picking your nose make your nostrils bigger?

example_sentences.japanese: 鼻の病気のせいでストレスが溜まっているからって、私たちに八つ当たりしないでよ！
example_sentences.english: Just because your nose issues are making you stressed, doesn’t mean that you have to take it out on us.

notes: "What do you get when you have four tens? You get forty." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. The only exception to this is 四, which uses the kun'yomi reading, since the on'yomi reading sounds too much like the word for ""death."" Luckily you know these reading already, so there's nothing new to learn!"

example_sentences.japanese: Tシャツを四十まいもっています。
example_sentences.english: I have forty T-shirts.

example_sentences.japanese: あの天才アメリカ人は四十才です。
example_sentences.english: That genius American is 40 years old.

example_sentences.japanese: 四十だいにもなると、ぜんしんがかゆい。
example_sentences.english: Since reaching my forties, my entire body has been itchy.

notes: "When you have four hundreds, you have four hundred." "This word has a number in it, so it uses the kun'yomi reading for it. But the reading for 百 is the on'yomi reading. This is pretty normal when it comes to counting numbers in Japanese. You know both of these readings already. Hooray!"

example_sentences.japanese: このしりょうを四百枚コピーしてください。
example_sentences.english: Please make four hundred copies of this document.

example_sentences.japanese: アメリカのシアトル市で、一やにして四百人がしっそうするというじけんがあった。
example_sentences.english: There was an incident where 400 people went missing overnight in the city of Seattle in the US.

example_sentences.japanese: いったいどうして四百ドルも一本の爪楊枝を買うのに使ったんだい？
example_sentences.english: How did you spend four hundred dollars on a toothpick?

english: Fourth Day, Day Four, Four Days
notes: "Fourth day or day four. No matter how you look at this combination of kanji, the meaning of the word makes a lot of sense!" "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Counting days, however, is an exception (at least up to ten). You need to use the kun'yomi readings to read this word. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 四, so that's fine (the ん gets turned into a small っ, though). Think of it this way:On the fourth day you pour yogurt (よっ) all over your car (か) because on the fifth day you're going to have to eat (いつ) it. (五's kun'yomi reading is いつ)."

example_sentences.japanese: らい月の四日に、わたしと一しょにやきゅうをみにいきませんか？
example_sentences.english: Why don’t you come watch baseball with me on the fourth of next month?

example_sentences.japanese: 七月四日はアメリカのどくりつきねん日です。
example_sentences.english: July 4th is Independence Day in America.

example_sentences.japanese: あのくまに出あって四日ご、ぼくのせなかにかびがはえた。
example_sentences.english: Four days after I met that bear, my back started growing mold.

notes: "Any number with a つ attached is a word that means ""NUMBER Things."" In this case, it's four things." "Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can assume it uses the kun'yomi reading. The ん part of よん gets converted to a small っ though, so watch out for that."

example_sentences.japanese: このはこには、みかんが四つあります。
example_sentences.english: There are four oranges in this box.

example_sentences.japanese: 小さい玉ねぎを四つ下さい。
example_sentences.english: Please give me four small onions.

example_sentences.japanese: 今朝、クロワッサンを四つか五つ食べました。
example_sentences.english: This morning, I ate four or five croissants.

notes: "You have four and you have thousand. Multiply them together and you have four thousand." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That's true for the 千 part, but the 四 reading is kun'yomi. You should know how to read this word as long as you've been studying your kanji!"

example_sentences.japanese: フォロワーが四千人になりました。
example_sentences.english: I hit four thousand followers.

example_sentences.japanese: これは、ちゅうごく四千ねんのれきしがつくり上げた、せかいに一つしかないとうふです。
example_sentences.english: This is the only tofu in the world created by China with great 4000 years of history.

example_sentences.japanese: 四千ぼんのでんちゅうをいっせいにたおせるくらい、きみのことをあいしているよ。
example_sentences.english: I love you so much that I could knock down four thousand telephone poles at once.

notes: "When you have a rest day you have a holiday." "This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note that the 日 reading is the alternate reading, じつ."

example_sentences.japanese: 休日は、えいがを見ることがおおいです。
example_sentences.english: I watched a bunch of movies over the holiday.

example_sentences.japanese: たのしい休日をすごしてくださいね。
example_sentences.english: Have a nice holiday!

example_sentences.japanese: 休日をツリーハウスで過ごした。
example_sentences.english: I spent the holiday in my tree house.

notes: "When a vocab word is a single kanji without okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it usually has the same meaning as the kanji it's spawned from. If you know the kanji meaning you'll also know the vocab meaning. It's one hundred!" When a vocab word is a single kanji with no okurigana, it usually uses the kun'yomi reading. Numbers are an exception to this. Numbers use the on'yomi reading, which you've already learned by learning the kanji's reading! How nice!

example_sentences.japanese: 一しゅうかんで、百ページよみました。
example_sentences.english: I read one hundred pages in one week.

example_sentences.japanese: 王子がレベル百になったら王か女王にてんしょくできますよ。
example_sentences.english: When you get to Level 100, Prince, you can change your job from prince to king or queen.

example_sentences.japanese: 百円で色々なものが買えるんですね。
example_sentences.english: I can buy a bunch of different things with a hundred yen.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading which is what you learned with the kanji.

example_sentences.japanese: 氷をつくっておいてください。
example_sentences.english: Please make the ice.

example_sentences.japanese: タピオカミルクティーを氷ぬきでちゅう文した。
example_sentences.english: I ordered a bubble tea without ice.

example_sentences.japanese: 「どうしてあの女は俺のグラスに氷を入れるのを忘れたんだ？」「彼女は今日自動車にひかれたんです。きっと飲み物を作っている時にまだふらふらしていたんだと思います。」
example_sentences.english: """Why did that woman forget to put ice in my glass?"" ""She was hit by a car earlier today. She must have been a little dizzy still while making your drink."""

notes: "The previous month is last month." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 先月、田中さんにあいました。
example_sentences.english: I met Tanaka last month.

example_sentences.japanese: 先月、市立びょういんであなたのお兄さんを見ましたよ。
example_sentences.english: I saw your older brother in the municipal hospital last month.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼らは先月コスプレパーティーをしました。
example_sentences.english: They had a cosplay party last month.

notes: "The past year is just last year." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 去年の四月に日本にきました。
example_sentences.english: I came to Japan in April of last year.

example_sentences.japanese: 去年、はじめて夏コミにさんせんしました。
example_sentences.english: Last year, I participated in the Summer Comiket for the first time.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はハンバーガーを毎日食べるので、去年よりも太ってしまった。
example_sentences.english: He is fatter than he was last year because he eats hamburgers every day.

notes: "A person whose name is known (because he's famous?). Why is this person's name known? Why is this person famous? It's because they are a master / expert at something. How else does someone become famous or well-known? That's pretty much it, even if they're just an expert at being an idiot." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: かれは、けんどうの名人です。
example_sentences.english: He is a kendo master.

example_sentences.japanese: かの女は、このくにに四人しかいないはいくの名人の一人です。
example_sentences.english: She is one of the four haiku masters in this country.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はチェスの名人であるだけでなく、トランプの名人でもある。
example_sentences.english: Not only is he an expert at chess, he’s also a master at cards.

notes: "one hundred ten thousands is how much? Multiply the two together and you get a million." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: このCDは、百万まいうれたそうです。
example_sentences.english: I heard that this CD sold a million copies.

example_sentences.japanese: WaniKaniで百万ドルもうけたので、きんでできたトーフグのおきものをつくるつもりです。
example_sentences.english: We are planning to make a Tofugu ornament made of gold with the million dollars we profited from WaniKani.

example_sentences.japanese: AKB48の裁判を見に、百万人の人々が法廷に出席した。
example_sentences.english: A million people attended the AKB48 court case.

english: Month Before Last, The Month Before Last
notes: "The previous previous month (remember that 々 just repeats the kanji before it) is the month before last." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 先々月、キューバにりょこうにいきました。
example_sentences.english: I took a trip to Cuba the month before last.

example_sentences.japanese: 先々月、シアトル市で大あめがふったせいで、市のめいぶつの玉ねぎばたけがぜんめつしてしまった。
example_sentences.english: Two months ago, due to the heavy rain in the city of Seattle, the city's famous onion field was entirely destroyed.

example_sentences.japanese: お母さんが先々月の携帯電話代を払ってくれた。
example_sentences.english: My mom paid my cellphone bill the month before last.

notes: "When you moon see something, you're doing a moon viewing." "The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. For 見 you already learned the kun'yomi reading when you learned the kanji. For 月 you'll have to think back to the vocab word 月 which uses the つき reading. Combine these two together and you have つきみ."

example_sentences.japanese: 月見のおだん子をつくっています。
example_sentences.english: I’m making rice dumplings for moon viewing.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日のよる、友人たちと、お月見をするよていです。
example_sentences.english: I am planning to have a moon viewing party with my friends tonight.

example_sentences.japanese: そ父は、月見の日に餅でのどを詰まらせて死にました。
example_sentences.english: My grandpa passed away from choking on a mochi cake on a moon viewing day.

notes: This vocabulary word is the same as the 'name' meaning of the kanji. If you can remember that, you'll have no trouble remembering this word as well. "Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: Just think of the first part of the English word name. What is it? It's na (な), just like this word!"

example_sentences.japanese: この花の名をおしえてください。
example_sentences.english: Please tell me the name of this flower.

example_sentences.japanese: きょ年のなつ、「きみの名は。」というえいがが日本ではやりました。
example_sentences.english: "Last summer, the movie ""Your Name"" became popular in Japan."

example_sentences.japanese: まだ彼女の名も知らない。
example_sentences.english: I still don’t know her name.

notes: "To remember the meaning of this word, just think about how in the olden days, before perforation was invented, people had to cut their postage stamps by hand. It took forever, especially if you had a lot of friends to mail things to. Be thankful that perforation was invented to save you time cutting them." "You'd think that the reading for this would consist of the on'yomi readings, but human body parts (hand) do funny things to words. In this case, it's the kun'yomi readings of both the kanji. You should know the kun'yomi reading for 切 and 手 from the previous levels, meaning you should be able to remember the reading for this word fairly easily. Watch out for the small っ, though."

example_sentences.japanese: それから、ゆうびんきょくへいって、切手をかいます。
example_sentences.english: Then I’m going to go to the post office and buy stamps.

example_sentences.japanese: あの外人さんは切手を一万まいもかっていったよ。
example_sentences.english: That foreigner bought 10,000 postage stamps.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女を失ってから、切手集めへの興味も失ってしまった。
example_sentences.english: Since I lost her, I've lost interest in stamp collecting.

notes: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

example_sentences.japanese: その赤のくつをとってください。
example_sentences.english: Please take the red shoes.

example_sentences.japanese: つぎは、まえがみのいろを赤にしようとおもっています。
example_sentences.english: I’m thinking of dyeing my bangs red next time.

example_sentences.japanese: オーランド・ブルームという名前を聞くだけで、今でも頬が赤くなる。
example_sentences.english: My cheeks still go red when I hear the name Orlando Bloom.

notes: "The two generation is the second generation." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: かれは、日けいアメリカ人二世の一人です。
example_sentences.english: He’s one of the second generation Japanese-Americans.

example_sentences.japanese: せいこうしている二世タレントは少ない。
example_sentences.english: Not many children of celebrities can be celebrities too.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は、父が日系イギリス人二世だということを知らなかった。
example_sentences.english: I didn’t know that my father is a second generation Japanese-Britain.

notes:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read this already.

The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. "The reading is the on'yomi reading which you learned with the kanji. This is probably because this word gets attached to numbers usually, which makes it behave more like jukugo. So, you can have １回, ２回, ３回, or even １００回 if you're into that sort of thing."

"A turtle shell that is patterned has much more effect and result and worth than a non-patterned turtle shell." "This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 甲 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:If you want to know how much you're worth, just take a look at your car (か). Cars are the result of money and hard work. So basically, they say how much you're worth!"

example_sentences.japanese: かえりに、貝をかってきましょうか。
example_sentences.english: Shall I buy clams on my way back?

example_sentences.japanese: 貝るいやこうかくるいをたべると、からだがかゆくなります。
example_sentences.english: My body gets itchy when I eat shellfish.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は、牡蠣の貝殻の中に置かれていることに気付かずに、婚約指輪を飲み込んでしまった。
example_sentences.english: I swallowed my engagement ring because I hadn’t noticed he put it in the oyster shell.

example_sentences.japanese: 日本に一回行ったことがあります。
example_sentences.english: I’ve been to Japan once.

example_sentences.japanese: アメリカから日本までおよいでわたるけいかくを立てたが、もう八回ほどと中で中止になっている。
example_sentences.english: I've made plans to swim from America to Japan, but they've been put on hold eight different times now.

example_sentences.japanese: 何回砂を食べたか自分でも数えきれないよ。
example_sentences.english: I can’t count the number of times I’ve eaten sand.

example_sentences.japanese: 努力の甲斐があって、そのニュースレターは廃刊になるのを免れた。
example_sentences.english: Thanks to his efforts, the newsletter was able to avoid being discontinued.

english: Small Plate, Small Dish, Little Plate, Little Dish
notes: "You have a small plate. Wait, is that it? Yep, that's it." "さら uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji, except it's ざら this time because of the rendaku. 小 uses an alternate kun'yomi reading. You can remember it by thinking ""What are small? Kids (子) are small. Bwahaha."""

example_sentences.japanese: 小皿をテーブルにならべてください。
example_sentences.english: Please set the small plates on the table.

example_sentences.japanese: かくじ、小皿にとり分けてたべましょう。
example_sentences.english: Why don't we just serve foods into small plates by ourselves and eat at our own pace?

example_sentences.japanese: このどでかいステーキを、その小皿に載せるのは無理だ。
example_sentences.english: It’s impossible to put this huge steak on that tiny dish.

notes: "When you have one writing letter what do you have? Here's a hint, there's one kanji in this word that consists of one writing letter (aka a straight line). " This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 女の子は、おこって口を一文字にむすびました。
example_sentences.english: The girl got angry and her mouth pursed into a straight line.

example_sentences.japanese: ペーパータオルでさかなの水気をふきとったら、かわに一文字の切り目を入れてください。
example_sentences.english: After wiping moisture off the fish with paper towels, score the skin straight across.

example_sentences.japanese: 白鳥たちは、うちの風呂場からその湖へ、真一文字になって飛んでいった。
example_sentences.english: The swans flew in a straight line from our bathtub to the lake.

notes: "You have one hit. What is (just) one hit? It is a strike or a blow." This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

example_sentences.japanese: ボールは、一打でグリーンにのりました。
example_sentences.english: The ball landed on the green in one stroke.

example_sentences.japanese: テニスでは、さいしょの一打を「サービス」とよびます。
example_sentences.english: "In tennis, a shot to start a point is called ""service."""

example_sentences.japanese: 一打逆転の大チャンスだ。
example_sentences.english: Just one hit would turn the tables in our favor.

notes: "Previous life... So we're talking about someone who has a previous life, or maybe previous life experience? When you have previous life experience, you can teach others about it, making you qualified to be some kind of teacher." This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生がアンナさんに手がみをかきました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher wrote a letter to Anna.

example_sentences.japanese: ダリン先生のつぎの休みはいつですか？
example_sentences.english: When is Dr. Darin's next day off?

example_sentences.japanese: 先生と生徒の恋愛についてどう思いますか？
example_sentences.english: What do you think of love between a student and a teacher?

hiragana: もうしもうし, もしもし
english: Telephone Hello, Hello, Hello On Telephone
notes: "It's kind of like you're saying say say. This is what you say when you answer or greet someone on the telephone. There's a strange story about this. One reason you say 申し申し is because it's hard for foxes to say. So, you're confirming that the other person isn't a fox. The other explanation is that operators would say this, letting the person know on the other line that they're talking by saying ""say say"" but in a humble way. Either way, this is a telephone hello, so say it next time you talk to someone on the phone who is Japanese... just to make sure they aren't a fox.We usually don't use kanji for this, so don't use it when you're writing. But you'll probably run into it in the wild so it's good to know!" This word uses the reading you learned with the kanji. You should know it already.

example_sentences.japanese: 申し申し、花子ちゃん？
example_sentences.english: Hello? Hanako?

example_sentences.japanese: あの、申し申し？きいていますか？？？
example_sentences.english: Hey, hello? Are you listening???

example_sentences.japanese: 「申し申し。鈴木と申しますが、佐藤さんはいらっしゃいますか？」
example_sentences.english: """Hello? This is Suzuki calling. Could I speak to Mr. Satou, please?"""
